title: THE BIBLE’S OLD TESTAMENT DIVORCE LAW WASN’T AS SIMPLE AS “MOSES APPROVED DIVORCE”
paragraphs: THE BIBLE’S OLD TESTAMENT DIVORCE LAW WASN’T AS SIMPLE AS “MOSES APPROVED DIVORCE”
What Jesus Said About Deuteronomy 24 Changes the Entire Conversation About Marriage, Divorce, Hard Hearts—and Grace
There is a sentence people have repeated so many times that it almost sounds like Scripture:
“Moses allowed divorce.”
And technically, Jesus Himself said Moses permitted it.
But if that is where you stop reading, you can walk away with almost the exact opposite impression Jesus intended.
Because when the Pharisees dragged Moses into their argument about divorce, Jesus did something remarkable.
He took them past Moses.
Past the certificate.
Past the legal debate.
Past the loopholes.
Past the question, “When am I allowed to leave?”
And He took them all the way back to a garden.
Back before divorce lawyers.
Back before certificates of separation.
Back before betrayal.
Back before adultery.
Back before abandoned spouses cried themselves to sleep.
Back before children learned what it felt like to divide Christmas between two homes.
Back before a husband looked at his wife and decided he wanted someone else.
Back before a wife looked at her husband and wondered where the man she married had gone.
Back before human beings became experts at finding biblical language for what hardened hearts already wanted to do.
Jesus went back to the beginning.
And perhaps that is where some of us need to go too.
Because the real scandal of Matthew 19 is not that Jesus made divorce difficult.
The scandal is that Jesus exposed what was hiding beneath the argument.
The Pharisees came asking about permission.
Jesus started talking about hearts.
They asked:
“Is it lawful?”
Jesus answered, in effect:
“What did God intend?”
Those are not always the same question.
And that difference changes everything.
Deuteronomy 24:1 contains words that have echoed through thousands of years of debate:
“כִּי־יִקַּח אִישׁ אִשָּׁה…”
Ki yiqqach ish ishah…
“When a man takes a woman as his wife…”
Then comes the difficult phrase:
“עֶרְוַת דָּבָר”
ʿervat davar.

The expression is notoriously difficult to capture with one English phrase. It has been rendered along the lines of “some indecency,” “something objectionable,” “some unseemly thing,” or, more literally, something involving “nakedness” or “indecency of a matter.”
Then comes another crucial expression:
“סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת”
sefer keritut.
A written document of severance—a certificate of divorce.
But here is where careless reading can quietly distort the passage.
Deuteronomy 24:1–4 is not simply God standing before Israel and saying, “Here is My wonderful institution of divorce. Go use it whenever marriage becomes inconvenient.”
The passage describes a tragic marital situation and places legal boundaries around what happens within it.

In the widely accepted grammatical reading of the passage, verses 1–3 form a long conditional scenario: a man marries a woman, divorce occurs, she receives the certificate and leaves, she marries another man, and that second marriage also ends through divorce or death.
Only then does the decisive prohibition arrive in verse 4.
The first husband may not simply take her back after that intervening marriage.
That observation matters enormously.
It means the text cannot responsibly be reduced to:
“God told men to divorce their wives.”
He did not.
And when Jesus was confronted with essentially that interpretation centuries later, He made the distinction unmistakable.
The Pharisees asked Him in Matthew 19:7:
“Why then did Moses command…?”
Notice their category.
Command.
But listen to Jesus.
Matthew records:
“Μωϋσῆς πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν ἐπέτρεψεν…”
Mōusēs pros tēn sklērokardian hymōn epetrepsen…
“Moses, because of your hardness of heart, permitted…”
Not commanded.
Permitted.
And then Jesus delivers the sentence that destroys every attempt to turn the concession into the ideal:
“ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως.”
Ap’ archēs de ou gegonen houtōs.
“But from the beginning it was not so.”
Read that again.
From the beginning…
it was not so.
Jesus does not deny Moses.
Jesus interprets Moses.
He tells us why such legislation existed in a fallen world.
“Because of your hardness of heart.”
The Greek word is devastating:
“σκληροκαρδία”
sklērokardia.
Hardness of heart.
This was never merely a paperwork problem.
It was a heart problem.
And suddenly this ancient argument becomes painfully modern.
Because human beings still do this.
We still ask God for the minimum obedience required while protecting the maximum amount of self-will possible.
“How far can I go before it becomes sin?”
“How much can I hate someone while technically forgiving them?”
“How little can I give and still call myself generous?”
“How much pornography can I watch before I admit I am enslaved?”
“How emotionally intimate can I become with someone who is not my spouse before I call it adultery?”
“How badly can I treat my husband or wife while insisting I never technically cheated?”
“When am I biblically allowed to leave?”
Sometimes the question sounds theological.
But underneath it may be another question entirely:
“God, how much of my own will can I keep?”
That is where Matthew 19 becomes uncomfortable.
Because Jesus refuses to let sinful humanity turn Scripture into a loophole factory.
The Pharisees wanted to discuss the exit.
Jesus discussed the covenant.
They wanted to discuss Moses.
Jesus quoted Genesis.
“Have you not read…?”
Then He reaches back to Genesis 1 and 2.
Male and female.
Leaving father and mother.
Holding fast.
Two becoming one flesh.
And then comes the thunder:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Marriage, in Jesus’ teaching, is not merely a human contract held together by romantic chemistry.
God is involved.
That changes the weight of everything.
The world says, “We fell out of love.”
Jesus reminds us that covenant cannot be reduced to the temperature of our emotions.
The world says, “I deserve someone who makes me happier.”
Jesus asks what faithfulness looks like when happiness becomes costly.
The world says, “Just follow your heart.”
Scripture warns us that hearts can become hard.
And yet…
this is where we must be extraordinarily careful.
Because someone reading these words has been betrayed.
Someone has been abandoned.
Someone has survived abuse.
Someone begged a spouse to stop committing adultery.
Someone fought for a marriage while the other person had already emotionally packed their bags.
Someone reading this is divorced and carries enough shame already.
Someone remarried years ago, came to Christ afterward, and now wonders whether God looks at their family with disgust.
Someone made terrible decisions.
Someone was sinned against terribly.
Someone was both wounded and guilty.
And if we preach Matthew 19 without the Gospel, we can turn the words of Jesus into stones.
That is not what this article is going to do.
Jesus does not minimize sexual betrayal.
Matthew 19:9 contains the famous exception involving:
“πορνείᾳ”
porneia.
Sexual immorality.

Christ's teaching is uncompromising about covenant faithfulness, and Christians have long wrestled carefully with the precise implications of His exception clause, remarriage, abandonment, separation, reconciliation, abuse, and pastoral application. Faithful Christian traditions do not agree on every downstream question.
So we should have enough humility not to pretend every difficult marriage can be solved with a slogan.
Nor should anyone use “God hates divorce” or “what God joined together” as a weapon to force a person to remain physically accessible to violence or immediate danger.
Biblical faithfulness never requires pretending evil is good.
Sin should be confronted.
The vulnerable should be protected.
Repentance should produce fruit.
Church leaders should take abuse, coercion, sexual betrayal, and danger seriously rather than hiding them behind religious language.
But neither should the existence of terrible situations become permission to rewrite Jesus into saying marriage is disposable.
Both errors are destructive.
One makes marriage an idol at the expense of wounded people.
The other makes personal fulfillment an idol at the expense of covenant.
Jesus does neither.
He tells the truth.
And truth sometimes cuts before it heals.
Maybe your marriage is not collapsing.
Maybe nobody has filed papers.
Maybe there has been no affair.
But maybe the divorce began emotionally years ago.
Two people under one roof.
Two phones glowing in separate rooms.
Two lives.
Two resentments.
Two people keeping records of wrongs.
No intimacy.
No prayer.
No tenderness.
No repentance.
Just survival.
You still wear the ring.
But somewhere inside, you stopped fighting for the person wearing the other one.
Maybe the hardest heart in Matthew 19 is not somebody else's.
Maybe it is yours.
Maybe yours became hard slowly.
One disappointment.
One insult.
One ignored apology.
One unresolved argument.
One secret conversation.
One fantasy.
One comparison.
One night sleeping back-to-back.
One morning when “I love you” disappeared.
Hard hearts rarely announce themselves.
They calcify quietly.
Until one day a person who once prayed, “God, thank You for giving me this person,” begins praying:
“God, give me permission to escape this person.”
And sometimes separation may indeed become tragically necessary.
Sometimes covenant has been grievously violated.
Sometimes wisdom, safety, church discipline, legal protection, or professional intervention becomes necessary.
But Jesus still forces us to ask the deeper question before we start searching for loopholes:
What happened to the heart?
That question reaches far beyond marriage.
Because sklērokardia is not just a divorce word.
It is a mirror.
You can remain married and have a hard heart.
You can be divorced and have a repentant heart.
You can quote Scripture and have a hard heart.
You can preach about family values and have a hard heart.
You can condemn adulterers while secretly feeding lust.
You can publicly defend biblical marriage while privately starving your spouse of affection, honor, tenderness, honesty, and repentance.
And you can have destroyed your marriage through your own sin…
and still encounter Jesus Christ.
That may be the sentence someone desperately needed to read.
Your sin can have consequences that cannot simply be reversed.
Deuteronomy 24 itself demonstrates that actions can create consequences that are not erased merely because someone later changes their mind.
But consequences are not the same thing as being beyond redemption.
The Gospel is not:
“Jesus came for everyone except people who ruined their marriage.”
The Gospel is that Christ came for sinners.
Adulterers.
Liars.
The sexually immoral.
The proud.
The bitter.
The selfish.
The abandoned.
The ashamed.
The religious hypocrite.
The broken spouse.
The guilty spouse.
People who stayed when they should have sought help.
People who ran when they should have stayed.
People whose stories became so tangled that they no longer know how to explain them without crying.
Jesus came for sinners.
That includes us.
Repentance does not mean pretending consequences disappear.
Grace does not mean calling evil good.
Forgiveness does not mean sin never mattered.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Sin mattered so much that the Son of God shed His blood.
But grace is so astonishing that the blood He shed is sufficient for sinners who come to Him.
That is why Christianity can look directly at human failure without surrendering to despair.
At the cross, God does not say:
“Your sin wasn't serious.”
He says:
“My Son is sufficient.”
Maybe your marriage survived.
Then do not read this article merely thinking about divorced people.
Go home softer.
Apologize first.
Put down the phone.
Stop flirting with temptation.
Stop keeping secret emotional doors open.
Tell the truth.
Pray together again.
Seek wise help before resentment becomes archaeology.
Do not wait until your marriage is bleeding out before admitting it has been wounded.
And if you are divorced?
Do not make divorce your permanent identity.
Your marital history is not your Savior.
Neither is your marital status.
Jesus is.
If you sinned, repent.
Not performatively.
Not vaguely.
Name what you did before God.
Where appropriate and safe, make amends without manipulating another person into restoring what your choices destroyed.
Accept consequences without believing consequences mean Christ has rejected you.
If you were sinned against, bring the wound to Jesus.
You do not have to pretend betrayal did not hurt in order to forgive.
You do not have to call abuse love.
You do not have to rewrite history.
You can tell the truth and still refuse to let bitterness become your new master.
And if your story is complicated?
Welcome to the human race.
The Bible is filled with complicated people.
People with sexual scandals.
Broken families.
Betrayals.
Failures.
Hard hearts.
Public shame.
Private tears.
And into that wreckage walks Jesus Christ.
Not carrying a broom to sweep your past under a religious rug.
Carrying a cross.
That is why our message has never been:
From scandal to pretending the scandal never happened.
It is:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing yesterday.
By redeeming the sinner standing here today.
That distinction matters.
Jesus can forgive your past without calling your past righteous.
Jesus can restore your soul even when some earthly consequences remain.
Jesus can teach a hard heart to become flesh again.
Jesus can teach a betrayed person to breathe again.
Jesus can teach a guilty person to repent instead of hide.
Jesus can teach a wounded church how to tell the truth without devouring its wounded.
And Jesus can take the sentence you thought ended your story and put a comma where you thought there was a period.
Maybe that is why this ancient divorce law matters so much.
Deuteronomy 24 shows us God entering a world where human relationships were already fractured and placing boundaries around human hardness.
Matthew 19 takes us deeper.
Jesus says:
Do not confuse God's regulation of human brokenness with God's original design.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
And then the Gospel takes us deeper still.
Because the One speaking those words would eventually be rejected Himself.
Betrayed.
Sold.
Abandoned.
Stripped.
Mocked.
Pierced.
Crucified.
And yet He loved.
Faithfully.
Covenantally.
Sacrificially.
To the end.
The Bridegroom gave Himself for His bride.
That is the center.
Not divorce.
Not marriage debates.
Not winning arguments about exception clauses.
Christ.
The faithful Christ.
The crucified Christ.
The risen Christ.
The Christ who tells sinners the truth and then invites them to come home.
So before you use Deuteronomy 24 to justify what you already want…
before you use Matthew 19 to crush someone whose story you barely understand…
before you point at your former spouse…
before you point at your current spouse…
before you point at the church…
put your hand over your own heart.
And ask:
“Jesus, has my heart become hard?”
That prayer could save more than a marriage.
It could save you from becoming someone you never imagined you would become.
Be honest.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Think about Jesus.
Think about the difference between permission and purpose.
Think about the terrifying possibility of a heart becoming hard while the mouth remains religious.
Then remember the breathtaking possibility that the same Christ who exposes hardness can transform the heart that finally stops hiding from Him.
Because your worst chapter does not have authority over the Author.
